learn.b: A struct bundles related variables, called members, under one name. It creates a new type you can use like int. The definition must end with a semicolon after the closing brace.
Create a variable of the struct type and fill it with braces in the order of the members. Use the dot operator to read or change a member.
Assigning a struct copies all its members, so the copy is independent of the original. You can pass a struct to a function and return one. For big structs, pass a const reference to avoid copying.
If you have a pointer to a struct, use the arrow operator -> to reach a member. p->x is the short form of (*p).x. Structs also go nicely in vectors, which lets you keep lists of records.
learn.code:
Point* q = &a;
std::cout << q->x;

learn.b: A class is like a struct that also holds functions, called methods, and can hide data. Members of a class are private by default, so code outside cannot touch them. Members of a struct are public by default.

Under public: the members are open to everyone. Under private: only the class's own methods can use them. Hiding data this way is called encapsulation, and it stops other code from putting the object in a bad state.
An object is a variable whose type is a class. Call its methods with a dot. Each object keeps its own copy of the data members.

Since the data is private, we give the class public methods to read it (getter) and change it (setter). A setter can check the new value first, for example refusing a negative age. A method that does not change the object can be marked const.
learn.code: int get() const { return n; }

learn.b: A constructor is a special method that runs automatically when an object is created. It has the same name as the class and no return type. It sets the object up with good starting values.
A neater way to set members is an initializer list after a colon. It sets the members before the body runs. It is required for const members and references.
learn.code: Car(int s) : speed(s) {}

learn.b: A constructor with no parameters is the default constructor. If you write no constructor at all, the compiler gives you one. If you write one with parameters, you must also write a default one if you want to create objects without arguments.

A destructor runs when an object is destroyed, for example at the end of its block. Its name is a tilde plus the class name, like ~Car(), and it takes no parameters. Objects in a block are destroyed in reverse order of creation. Destructors clean up things like open files or memory.

learn.b: Operator overloading lets your own types work with operators like +, == and <<. You write a function whose name is the word operator followed by the symbol. It should do what people expect from that symbol.
Once defined, the operator is used like with built-in types. V r = V{2} + V{5}; calls your function. This makes code short and readable, but only overload when the meaning is obvious.
learn.code:
V r = V{2} + V{5};
std::cout << r.x;  // 7

learn.b: Overload == to compare objects and return a bool. To print with cout, overload << as a normal function taking an ostream reference and returning it so chaining works.

An operator can also be a member function, where the left operand is the object itself, as in M operator*(int k). You cannot invent new symbols like **, and you cannot change precedence or the number of operands. Cannot overload :: . or sizeof.

learn.b: Inheritance lets a new class reuse an existing one. A Dog is an Animal, so Dog can inherit from Animal. The class you inherit from is the base class and the new one is the derived class.

The derived class has all the public and protected members of the base. Private members of the base exist but cannot be used directly by the derived class. protected means visible to the class and its children but not to the outside.

Creating a derived object first runs the base constructor, then the derived one. Destruction goes the other way: derived destructor first, then base. If the base needs arguments, call it in the initializer list.

A derived class can add new members and new methods. Always write public before the base name for a normal is-a relationship. Use inheritance only when the is-a sentence makes sense, otherwise prefer having one class as a member of another.

learn.b: A base class pointer can point to a derived object. But a normal method call through that pointer uses the base version, because the compiler decides by the pointer type. That is usually not what we want.
learn.code:
Animal* a = &dog;
a->speak();  // base version without virtual

learn.b: Mark the base method virtual and the program decides at runtime which version to call, based on the real object. In the derived class write override after the function, so the compiler checks that it really replaces a virtual one.
A pure virtual function is declared with = 0 and has no body. A class with at least one is abstract, and you cannot create objects of it. It works like a contract that derived classes must fulfil.

If you delete a derived object through a base pointer, the base destructor must be virtual, or the derived part is never cleaned up. Any class meant to be a base should have a virtual destructor. This is polymorphism: one interface, many behaviours.

learn.b: A function template is a blueprint. You put template <typename T> before it, and T stands for any type. The compiler writes a real version for each type you use.

Usually the compiler works out T from the arguments, so twice(4) uses int and twice(2.5) uses double. You can also write the type yourself, like twice<double>(4). Both arguments of one T must have the same type.
learn.code:
std::cout << twice(4);    // 8
std::cout << twice(1.5);  // 3

learn.b: Classes can be templates too. std::vector is one. You give the type in angle brackets when you create an object, and each type gives a separate class.

Templates are filled in at compile time, so there is no slowdown at runtime. Template code usually lives completely in header files. Error messages can be long, so read the first line and the line number of your own code.

learn.b: std::map from <map> stores key and value pairs sorted by key. Use m[key] to read or write a value. If the key does not exist, m[key] creates it with a default value like 0. m.size() counts the pairs.
std::set from <set> stores unique values in sorted order. Inserting a value that is already there does nothing. s.count(x) tells you whether x is in the set by giving 1 or 0.

std::unordered_map from <unordered_map> works like map but uses hashing. Lookups are usually faster, but the order of the keys is not defined. Choose it when you only need quick lookup and do not care about order.
A range-based for loop visits every element. For a map each element is a pair with .first for the key and .second for the value. A set gives its values in sorted order.

learn.b: An iterator points to an element of a container. v.begin() points to the first element and v.end() points one past the last. You read the element with * and move on with ++. An iterator equal to end means there is nothing there.

A lambda is a small unnamed function written inline. It starts with [ ] for captured variables, then parameters, then the body. Put a variable in the brackets to use its value inside.
learn.code:

std::cout << f(4);  // 8

    [](int x) { return x > 2; });

learn.b: Normal variables disappear at the end of their block. For data that must live longer, you ask for memory on the heap with new. new gives you a pointer, and you must free it with delete when you are done. Forgetting is a memory leak.
new int[3] makes an array on the heap, and you free it with delete[] with square brackets. Mixing delete and delete[] is a bug. Never use a pointer after you have deleted it.
A std::unique_ptr from <memory> owns one heap object and deletes it automatically when it goes out of scope. Create it with std::make_unique. It cannot be copied, because only one owner is allowed.
learn.code:
auto p = std::make_unique<int>(9);
std::cout << *p;

learn.b: A std::shared_ptr lets several owners share one object. It counts the owners with use_count() and deletes the object when the last owner is gone. Make one with std::make_shared. Prefer smart pointers over raw new and delete in modern C++.

learn.b: An exception is a way for code to signal that something went wrong. You put risky code in a try block. When code runs throw, the rest of the try block is skipped and the matching catch block runs.
Include <stdexcept> and throw objects like std::runtime_error with a message. Catch them by const reference to std::exception and print the message with e.what().

If a function throws and does not catch, the exception travels up to the caller, then its caller, until a catch matches. If nobody catches it, the program stops. This keeps error handling out of the normal logic.
learn.code:
void f() { throw 5; }
// the caller can catch it

learn.b: Catch blocks are checked from top to bottom, and the first matching one runs, so put specific types first. catch (...) catches anything and goes last. Use exceptions for real errors, not for normal flow.

learn.b: Include <fstream>. std::ofstream writes to a file and std::ifstream reads from one. They use << and >> just like cout and cin. The file closes when the object goes out of scope, or when you call close().
To read a file line by line, loop with while (std::getline(in, line)). The loop stops at the end. Always check that the file opened with if (!in), since it may be missing.

Big programs are split into files. A header file .h holds declarations, like function prototypes and class definitions. A .cpp file holds the definitions. Any file that needs them writes #include "util.h" with quotes. Put #pragma once at the top of a header so it is not included twice.

Compile every .cpp file and link them together in one command. g++ main.cpp util.cpp -o app builds a program called app. -o names the output. Add -std=c++17 to choose the language version and -Wall to see more warnings. Run the result with ./app.
learn.code:
g++ -std=c++17 main.cpp util.cpp -o app
./app
